title: Thinking Inside the Box
series: Thinking Inside the Box, an illustrated essay on whether large language models make people think worse
style: warm white paper, a thin grey pen line, one sky-blue watercolour with granulation and pooled edges, small faceless figures in white dresses, translucent cubes and other solids standing for the machine's thought, Cormorant Garamond display type and IBM Plex Mono labels
context: The video asks whether large language models make people think worse, following the essay Thinking Inside the Box. Key studies. Bastani et al. 2025 (PNAS, peer reviewed): about 1,000 Turkish high-school students randomised by class; practising with a plain ChatGPT-style interface raised practice scores 48% (a hint-only 'GPT Tutor' version 127%); on the closed-book exam without the tool the plain-ChatGPT students scored 17% lower than students who never had it, while the hint-only group was about the same as control ('largely mitigated'). Shen & Tamkin 2026 (Anthropic, preprint RCT, 52 junior developers): quiz 50% with an AI assistant vs 67% without, 17 points, d = 0.74, no significant speed gain. Kosmyna et al. 2025 (MIT Media Lab, arXiv preprint 'Your Brain on ChatGPT'): 54 people, 18 per group (ChatGPT, search engine, brain only), 18 in a fourth crossover session; 0 of 18 ChatGPT writers could quote their own essay correctly minutes later vs 15 and 16 of 18; EEG connectivity 'up to 55%' lower in the ChatGPT group (a maximum over bands); the critique by Stanković et al. 2025 says about 159 participants were needed; the authors' FAQ says 'No!' to 'making us dumber' and asks journalists not to use 'stupid', 'dumb', 'brain rot', 'harm', 'damage'. Lee et al. 2025 (CHI, Microsoft Research, 319 knowledge workers, 936 examples): confidence in the AI predicts less critical thinking (beta −0.69), self-confidence predicts more (beta +0.26), self-report. METR 2025 RCT: 16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks, 19% slower with AI tools (95% CI +2 to +39%) while believing they were 20% faster; a 2026 follow-up found a small uncertain speed-up. Peng et al. 2023: 95 developers 55.8% faster with Copilot, guessed 35%. Dell'Acqua et al. 2023 (758 BCG consultants): quality up about 40% inside the model's competence; outside it, about a fifth less likely to be correct (84% vs 60–70%); ideas 41% less diverse. Doshi & Hauser 2024 (Science Advances, 293 writers, 600 readers): with five AI ideas novelty +8.1%, usefulness +9.0%, stories 8.9–10.7% of the similarity range more alike. Melumad & Yun 2025 (PNAS Nexus, 10,462 people): advice after learning from an LLM shorter, rated less helpful, similarity 0.159 vs 0.057. Stadler et al. 2024: lower cognitive load, worse reasoning, no narrowing. Fan et al. 2025: better essays, no more learning ('metacognitive laziness'). Kestin et al. 2025 (Scientific Reports, Harvard, 194 students): a scaffolded GPT-4 tutor beat an active-learning class by 0.63 (linear) to 0.73–1.3 (quantile) standard deviations in 49 vs 60 minutes; human tutors average d = 0.79 (VanLehn 2011); Bloom's 2 sigma came from two dissertations. Lehmann et al. 2025: explanation-seeking +0.25 understanding, solution-seeking −0.31. Costello, Pennycook & Rand 2024 (Science, 2,190 people): dialogue with GPT-4 reduced conspiracy belief about 20%, lasting two months, 99.2% of the model's claims true. Mechanism: Bjork's desirable difficulties (storage strength vs retrieval strength); generation effect d = 0.40 (Bertsch 2007, 86 studies); Roediger & Karpicke 2006: re-reading 83% vs tested 71% at five minutes, 40% vs 61% a week later, re-readers most confident; expertise reversal (worked examples help novices, hurt those with a schema); Bainbridge 1983 'a formerly experienced operator who has been monitoring an automated process may now be an inexperienced one'; Arthur et al. 1998 skill decay d = −1.4 after a year of disuse; Budzyń et al. 2025 (Lancet Gastro): endoscopists' unassisted detection fell 28.4% to 22.4% after three months with AI; Risko & Gilbert 2016 offloading drift. History: Plato's Phaedrus c. 370 BCE, Thamus: writing 'will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls'; Gessner 1545 'confusing and harmful abundance of books'; reading mania 1790s; the telephone caused no panic; Minow 1961 'vast wasteland'; calculators: Hembree & Dessart 1986, 79 studies, 529 effect sizes, better paper-and-pencil skills at every grade but the fourth; Sparrow 2011 Google effect, its priming experiment failed to replicate in 2018; Carr 2008; Dahmani & Bohbot 2020 GPS r about −0.2, self-rating r = 0.07; FAA SAFO 13002 (2013) on autoflight and skill degradation; Air France 447; Oxford word of the year 2024 'brain rot', first used by Thoreau 1854. Adoption: ChatGPT 100 million users in two months (Jan 2023), 400 M weekly (Feb 2025), 800 M (Oct 2025), 900 M (Feb 2026); UK undergraduates using generative AI 66% (2024), 92% (2025), 95% (2026), for assessed work 94%; US teens using chatbots for schoolwork 54% (2025), one in ten do all or most; 34% of US adults have used ChatGPT, 58% under 30; Pew 2025: 53% expect AI to worsen creative thinking. Responses: NYC schools banned ChatGPT Jan 2023 and lifted it May 2023; Anthropic Learning mode Apr 2025; OpenAI Study Mode Jul 2025; Pope Leo XIV, Nov 2025: 'Use it in such a way that if it disappeared tomorrow, you would still know how to think.' The essay's answer: not dumber; worse at the thing you let the tool do for you, while you let it, and unable to feel the difference; the harm disappears when the tool hints, explains or argues instead of answering.
